and that would fit everybody else in the entire world who was size medium. But about a year later, I got a call from one of the old South Virginia teammates, and Jim had been found dead in his apartment. He had apparently the pituitary gland issue was a little touchier than he led on to me to believe. And sometime over the weekend when he was living alone,

something had gone awry with the chemistry, and he hadn't been able to get help, and he passed away. And I can't remember what it was. I want to think it was something like snow, and I had sheep who were having lambs, and I was living alone or something, but for some reason I didn't go to the memorial.

But I think the real reason was that this time I couldn't bear to go. One time, I would get back down to the beach every once in a while. Every few years I'd get back down there. But I had been having, since my sister hadn't been talking to me, I had my mom's ashes,

and I hadn't done anything with them because I thought, you know, we should do something together, but she didn't talk to me. So it took about five years, and finally I decided, well, I guess I've got to do something anyway. So I got together with my brother

and took my son down, and we went to the beach, and we went back to the cabin, which my brother had owned after my mom died for a while, but he had to sell it, so we ended up renting it from whoever owned it. And we spread the ashes in the ocean,

and I built a really beautiful wooden urn that we burned on the beach. And in the last moments of burning it, this fluorescent green light came out of the middle of it and just stayed there for a full minute, and we had no idea what it could have been. Another time, a few years later,

going down to the beach, heading to the cabin with a girlfriend, stopped into the Copeland's Lumber Store at the edge of town, a couple miles from the cabin to pick up something I knew I needed there, and said to the girl at the counter, hey, has John Pound been around recently?

And she just blanched. She told me that John had shot himself a couple weeks before that he had cancer, and I never really found out any other details. I didn't really want to know any other details. And then a few years after that, going down to the beach again with another girlfriend,

trying to go to the cabin again, but hadn't been able to call anybody who still owned it, and so we just got a different place to rent, but I thought I'd show it to her, and drove right by where it was, missed it, came back, and found out that some developer

had bought up a bunch of cabins in that row and torn them down to the ground and had built this ugly shoebox of a thing where the cabin used to be, so it's gone. Well, around that time that I was getting divorced and all of this, I basically was having a pretty hard time,

and Norman sort of went to bat for me, and it was the very first year that they did the January practice period at Green Gulch, and I thought that would be a good thing if I just got out of town and went down there, so I think he needed some sort of prerequisite,

but he sort of squeezed me in the door at that point, and that was a good time to be able to be there and practice, and that was where I met Michael Newton from Vancouver, because Michael sat right next to me all month, and also we were on the same work cruise and had all the same schedule, basically.

So that brings us up close to the present. A couple years ago, probably it would be interesting to know, there was a South Eugene Track reunion. It was a surprise for Harry Johnson on his retirement from Nike. He thought he was going to meet two or three people for dinner,

but instead there were 200 athletes from the 70s who met him for a huge banquet, and we took all the old Super 8 movies that he took of us running and converted them to DVDs and had them playing up there, and Steve, Billy's brother, spoke first, and I remember the very first thing he said was,

who are all those little kids up there? Because we did. We thought of ourselves as men, but boy, we just looked like little teenagers, and I remember I spoke. They had all the team captains from the different years speak, and one of the things I remember saying was,

this is really great because we never get to talk about these years in our lives today, because who wants to hear about The track at South Eugene got refurbished. Jeff is the coach there now, and he did a huge half a million dollar fundraising campaign.

So the track that when I first ran on it in seventh grade that was cinders and then that Harry first surfaced with rubberized asphalt where we set all the national records has been refurbished now, and it's the Tom and Bill McChesney Memorial Track, and it's become an integral part

of the new era of Olympic trials in Eugene because as part of their bid for the trials, they include the idea that the South Eugene track will be the practice track for all the athletes. So that's been a really nice turn of events, but I think it took at least 10 or 12 or more years after Billy's death

for us to be able to all come together again that way. It just took a long, long time, and now we can talk about those people, but for a long time it felt just too hard. Well, that's pretty much the end of my talk. Thanks for allowing me to take a lot of extra time

than maybe some people do with these talks. I felt like I had a lot of things to say, so I hope it was okay, I hope it was good to hear, and I feel especially honored to be able to choose so for this group. This is a really special group, and it feels like we're in a really special time
of building a really strong sangha. So thank you.
